newsitem.title: USA: Rising Mississippi River threatens Louisiana.
newsitem.headline: Rising Mississippi River threatens Louisiana.

text.p: Louisiana officials were scrambling to sandbag weak points in levees and build tent cities for prisoners on Friday as the flood-swollen Mississippi River pushed toward a near-record crest.
Federal officials said the predicted 44-foot (13.4 metre) crest at Baton Rouge on March 27 would be the highest since 1945, when the river reached 45.18 feet (13.77 metres).

In downtown Baton Rouge, prisoners were filling sandbags for a 500-foot (152 metre) long, 3-foot (0.9 metre) high extension of the levee near the historic old state capitol where the river is expected to crest at the same height as the levee, Corps of Engineers spokesman Rob Brown told Reuters.

Upriver from the city at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola, rifle-toting guards supervised inmate sandbagging operations as seepage from "sand boils" was undermining 55 locations along the 21 miles (33.8 km) of levees that surround three sides of the 18,000-acre (7,280 hectare) prison, Warden Burl Cain told Reuters.

Prison authorities, aided by the Louisiana National Guard, also began constructing two tent cities on Thursday to house the prison's 4,900 maxiumum-security inmates if the river broke its banks, he said.
One tent compound will be located on high ground at the prison, while the second is being erected on state-owned land across from an elementary school in nearby Tunica, La.
West Feliciana Parish Sheriff Bill Daniel said the schoolchildren would be moved if prisoners were brought in.
Cattle trucks, cotton trailers and other farm equipment, attached to tractors are on stand-by to move prisoners to high ground if a levee breaks.
"We'll get them with boats if we have to," Cain said.

Swift currents accompanying the rising waters convinced the Corps of Engineers to begin opening the Bonnet Carre Spillway near Laplace, La., upriver from New Orleans, on Monday to relieve pressure on levees guarding the city and to lessen the current for marine traffic.

After several accidents on the river this week, the Coast Guard issued temporary restrictions on traffic south from Vicksburg, La., by limiting the number of barges allowed under tow at any given time and requiring deep draft vessels to take additional precautions to avoid ramming into levees.

An accident on Monday two miles (3.2 km) upriver from Baton Rouge continued to restrict river traffic to one-way one vessel-at-a-time, as federal, state and local officials tried on Friday to determine how to safely unload a volatile cargo of benzene and gasoline from a capsized barge.

The Corps objected to plans to drill holes in the hull to measure vapour pressure inside the barge, which is pushed up against the west bank of the river across from the city, because an explosion could blow a hole in the main levee.
"We don't want anything done where it is now," Corps civil engineer Jason Binet told Reuters.
